en: Semetey, my dear, unbred noble steed,
The pennant fixed upon my spear,
The gift left by magnanimous Manas!
My orphan, shall I see you?
‘If only I see you, my only one,’ I said.
Little time remains before I die.
My rooted plane tree, my refuge,
My cherished dear one,
Who fled to Bukhara,
My dark, white-marked hawk,
‘Will my orphan come?’ I wondered,
And burned with longing for you.
Because of the troublemakers,
I scattered this treasure of mine.
When you were a babe in the cradle,
May I take your misfortune upon myself,
My one who fled toward Bukhara.
From my only son, dark wolf-maned Manas,
You are the lion I held on to.
When you went to Bukhara,
I spent my treasure and livestock.
‘Will my support, my darling camel-calf, come?’ I wondered,
And begged God for you with all my heart.
I went on long in grief without dying.
The poor orphan left by rascal Manas,
I kept wondering whether he would come.
Offering prayers to Baabedin,
I spent everything I had.
When my Manas comes to mind,
I grieve worse than anyone.
‘May my orphan come safely,’ I say,
And go on asking for you in this world.”
Then his grandfather Khan Zhakyp
Wept with ringing cries,
Pretended to wail and lament.
Pretending to lament, he beat himself,
Falsely wept over the boy and pleaded.
He drew him close;
His mouth touched him colder than a club.
“Rise, senior wife, rise,” he said.
“Is there any of that cursed drink?
Pour some for this child of mine,” he said.
The senior wife sprang up.
The sweet drink mixed with honey
She poured for Khan Bakai.
Bakai began to swallow it.
The bitter drink mixed with poison,
With burning poison mingled in it,
The senior wife brought and offered,
And stood not knowing what to do.
Without speaking a word,
“Give it to your grandfather, the swine khan,”
She then indicated with gestures.
Flicking her brows, winking,
Biting her lip, shaking her head,
“Give it to your grandfather,”
She gestured without a sound.
The senior wife Bagdoolot
Used this stratagem.
Taking the liquor, Semetey,
“Grandfather,” he pleaded,
And offered it to Khan Zhakyp.
Refusing to drink, he babbled foolishly;
God struck Zhakyp astray.
“Grandfather, if I drink before you,
And then drink away my faith with it,
Could I prosper if I drank without offering it?
If you, my khan grandfather, do not taste it first,
Would it be right for me to drink?
Could I grow complete and prosper?
If I drink without offering it to you,
Could I ever prosper?
With no post to tether a horse,
If I drink before you,
I shall be utterly destitute.
Without seeing the face of God,
Grandfather, I shall become an infidel.
If I drink your refreshment without a word,
Will I reach maturity?
If I drink before you,
Will I see next autumn?
You planted me and made a garden;
You built me and made a house.
One who drinks before his father,
Who drinks away all his honor with it—
Can such a one be a child?
Could anyone calling him a child prosper?
If that child has no honor,
Could he ever prosper?
Drink yourself, grandfather, drink yourself!”
So saying, Semetey
Offered his bowl back.
Then Zhakyp said:
“I will not drink, my child, I will not drink.
When my foal Manas died,
When this head of mine suffered calamity,
When my upright back was broken,
Bereft of my khan son,
When God struck me into darkness,
When I settled along the valley,
Bereft of my falcon,
When I was like a fire gone out,
When my sharp Narkesken was bent,
Bereft of my only one, Khan Manas,
When my black eyes were dimmed—
O child, I have something to tell you.
This cursed liquor,
If I drink it, my foal,
May I eat my camel-calf's liver,
May I declare there are two Gods!
With nothing amassed in this world,
And dying without faith,
I said I would become these if I drank.
I laid a curse upon myself.
When my falcon Manas died,
I swore not to drink,
Made an oath upon my death.
I made my promise firm.
Not once concerning this drink,
Forty-two times I swore.
Your grandfather Khan Zhakyp
Was ninety-eight years old.
This was the drink I vowed not to drink.
Swallow it, my son Semetey,
My light who has come thirsty,
My orphan who has come parched.
Drinking it quenches thirst;
Sleeping brings rest to the soul.
My cherished treasure left by Manas,
My morning star left by my son,
My spring in the valley of Keng-Kol,
Drink, my child, drink,
My dear one found late in life!
When young men like you drink kumys and grow merry,
Young and wild of spirit,
Who would not drink this?
Drink it down, my child, drink it down!
When drinking liquor, merry,
Young and light of mind,
Who would hold back from liquor?
Liquor is a warrior's companion.
Take it, my child, take it!”
The wretched baldhead would not change;
He kept pressing his arguments.
He urged him on relentlessly.
“Drink,” said Khan Zhakyp,
Urging Semetey then.
Manas's son, brave Semen,
To Temir Khan's city
Had wandered and grown up.
Your warrior knew proper conduct.
“Ah, my grandfather, Khan Zhakyp,
Who could drink before you
This drink you have offered?
If you will not drink, let a dog drink.
If no dog drinks, let a bird drink.
Let the pitch-dark night drink.
Who else could drink it?
Khan grandfather, crookedness lies in your eyes.
If you find your chance, grandfather,
You mean to do away with me.
Ill intent lies in your eyes;
Evasiveness lies in your words.
Offering your choking poison to me,
Khan grandfather, you mean to slaughter me.
If you could, in Talas
You would make me gather dung.
My strength has come; hand over
Khan Manas's turn to me.
When my khan father Manas died,
You plundered his treasury,
And put on his fox-fur coat.
God willing, I shall end
The laughter of your six sons.
Calling you grandfather, I came to you.
You are a creature of hell,
Calling you my forefather, I came to you.
Must you avenge your father upon me,
That you singled me out for your poison?
Taking up the bowl,
The warrior born of Manas
Flung it toward the threshold.
It splashed at the wall's foot.
When the liquor reached there,
The gray male dog with a leather-pail head,
That hound of Zhakyp's—
Know the poison's strength by this:
He did not survive smelling it.
His neck drew back, and he was gone.
When the gray dog died,
His grandfather Zhakyp's
Swinish nature he now knew.
His khan grandfather Zhakyp
He now knew to be an enemy.
“My wretched grandfather, you will never change.
Giving poison to your own child,
If you go on like this,
You will not be a true Muslim.
To Temir Khan's city
I wandered and grew up.
To Temir Khan's city,
On whose account did I wander?
It was on your account, grandfather.
To the city of the many Sarts,
On whose account did I flee?
On your account, my hellish grandfather!
Were it not for the trouble you caused,
Should a prince's only son
Have to live in flight?
Your bestial nature is all too true.
Khan grandfather, is there a grave that will admit you?
Should a nobleman's camel-calf
Have to wander in exile?
If your nobility is true,
Valiant grandfather, listen:
Where are the people in this Talas?
You brought ruin upon my lineage.
Where did you send away
My people in this Talas?
You spoke words of discord.
Your rage boiling, khan grandfather,
You meant to destroy me,
Meant to wipe me out.
You prepared your liquor and food.
You meant to dig my pit,
Meant to brew up
My terrible misery, khan grandfather.
You meant to show me
Wonders no human should see.
Now I shall draw a line for you.
If it is a quarrel you desire,
Let me begin turmoil against you.
At the horses you refuse when asked,
Khan grandfather, let me cast a cold lasso.
The wealth you refuse when requested,
Let me openly seize it.
Let me strip away your strength.
Let me seize back every beast,
My livestock left by my khan father Manas.
Grandfather, with a golden collar and bronze sleeves,
Double mail with links like larks' eyes,
No bullet can pierce it in battle,
Akolpok, left by my father—
Grandfather Zhakyp, where is it?
Long ago, at Kokotai's memorial feast,
Infidels and Muslims
Gathered together there.
Karacha's Khan Saikal
Freely gave the roan horse.
That inheritance from my father, where is it?
Just last autumn,
On the plain beyond Alai,
Sixty Russian surveyors,
Dragging their wagons,
Came from far away,
Wearing their yellow coats,
